triage.name: Hypomagnesemia
triage.reason: Common electrolyte abnormality that presents with nonspecific symptoms and arrhythmias; diagnosis is made by history, medication review and serum magnesium.

demographics: More common in hospitalized patients, especially those in intensive care
More common in people with alcohol use disorder
More common in older adults, partly because of diuretic use and reduced intake

risk_factors.text: Proton pump inhibitor use, especially long-term

comorbidities: Gastroesophageal reflux disease on long-term acid suppression
family_history: Rare inherited tubulopathies causing renal magnesium wasting (e.g., Gitelman syndrome)

chief_complaints.text: I feel weak and tired all the time
My heart feels like it is fluttering or skipping

hpi.onset: Gradual, often noticed only when magnesium is checked during an illness or hospitalization
hpi.duration: Days to weeks; chronic in people on long-term diuretics or acid suppression
hpi.progression: Symptoms are vague at first and worsen as magnesium falls; severe deficiency can cause tetany, seizures or arrhythmia
hpi.location: Generalized; muscle symptoms are most noticeable in the legs, hands and around the mouth
hpi.quality: Aching, cramping, twitching and a sense of generalized weakness
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate for most; severe with tetany, seizures or arrhythmia
hpi.timing: Often worse at night or after exertion; may be constant

associated_symptoms.text: Tingling around the mouth or in the hands and feet

pertinent_negatives: Focal weakness or numbness in a single limb
Known seizure disorder with a typical pattern

positives.text: Tingling around the mouth or in the hands and feet

atypical.how_it_differs: Symptoms are often attributed to aging or other chronic illness; weakness, confusion and falls may be the only clues, and arrhythmia risk is higher.
May present with irritability, poor feeding, vomiting, muscle twitching or seizures rather than clear cramps.
Leg cramps and nausea are common in pregnancy, so hypomagnesemia may be missed; severe deficiency can cause tetany or preterm contractions.
Magnesium wasting from tubular injury or diuretics can coexist with kidney disease; symptoms may be masked by uremia and magnesium replacement must be monitored closely.
missing_classic_features: Clear temporal relationship to low intake

atypical.how_it_differs: Osmotic diuresis from hyperglycemia causes renal magnesium loss; symptoms overlap with hypoglycemia and neuropathy.

general.mild: Comfortable, no distress; subtle findings only
general.moderate: Mildly uncomfortable, reports cramps or twitching
general.severe: Ill-appearing, restless, visibly twitching or cramping
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, confused or obtunded, may be seizing or in tetany

findings.maneuver: Assess strength and observe the patient's spontaneous movement
Ask about and observe for spontaneous muscle cramping
findings.finding: Painful muscle cramps, often in the legs or hands

findings.maneuver: Observe the muscles at rest for spontaneous fasciculation
Inflate a blood pressure cuff above systolic pressure on the arm for 3 minutes
findings.finding: Carpal spasm with wrist and metacarpophalangeal flexion

findings.maneuver: Tap the facial nerve just anterior to the ear over the mandible
findings.finding: Twitching of the ipsilateral facial muscles

findings.maneuver: Observe the hands and feet during a symptomatic episode
findings.finding: Carpopedal spasm with flexion of the wrists and ankles

findings.maneuver: Test the deep tendon reflexes at the biceps, brachioradialis, patella and Achilles
findings.finding: Brisk or hyperactive deep tendon reflexes

findings.maneuver: Ask about and test for tingling around the mouth or in the hands and feet
Observe for and ask about witnessed convulsive activity
Palpate the radial pulse and auscultate the heart
findings.finding: Irregularly irregular rhythm suggesting atrial fibrillation

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the heart and count the rate
Measure the blood pressure with the patient seated or supine
Inspect the internal jugular vein with the patient at 45 degrees
Perform a focused neurologic exam including strength, sensation, and cranial nerves
findings.finding: No focal weakness, sensory loss, or cranial nerve abnormality

findings.maneuver: Assess neck stiffness and perform Brudzinski and Kernig maneuvers if meningeal signs are suspected
findings.finding: No neck stiffness or meningeal signs

labs.caveat: Serum magnesium is the diagnostic test; it underestimates total body stores, so normal levels do not fully exclude deficiency.
Hypokalemia is common and often refractory until magnesium is replaced.
Hypocalcemia often accompanies hypomagnesemia and may not correct until magnesium is repleted.
Hyponatremia may coexist with diuretic use or volume depletion.
Elevated creatinine suggests renal magnesium wasting or coexisting kidney injury and affects replacement dosing.
Low bicarbonate suggests metabolic alkalosis from diuretics or vomiting, or a renal tubulopathy such as Gitelman syndrome.
Hyperglycemia with glycosuria causes osmotic renal magnesium loss.
Low albumin from malnutrition or alcohol use lowers total calcium and magnesium measurements.
Check when no cause is found; hypothyroidism can cause muscle cramps and weakness.
High specific gravity suggests volume depletion; a high urine magnesium with low serum magnesium points to renal wasting.

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected renal cause of magnesium wasting or coexisting kidney disease

findings.text: Small echogenic kidneys suggesting chronic kidney disease

initial.why: Confirms the diagnosis and grades severity
Checks potassium, calcium, bicarbonate and kidney function, which guide replacement
Adds phosphorus and ionized calcium when the basic panel is not enough
Looks for QT prolongation and arrhythmia, which change urgency

supporting.why: Urine magnesium and specific gravity help separate renal wasting from poor intake
supporting.only_if: the cause is unclear after history and medication review

supporting.why: Screens for hypothyroidism when no cause is found
Interprets total calcium and magnesium when malnutrition or alcohol use is present

not_indicated.why: Not routine; reserve for suspected obstruction or structural kidney disease
not_indicated.only_if: obstruction or structural renal disease is suspected

not_indicated.why: Not needed to diagnose hypomagnesemia unless another illness is suspected
No role unless abdominal pain suggests pancreatitis
No role unless meningitis or encephalitis is suspected

decision_points: Check magnesium in any patient with unexplained hypokalemia, hypocalcemia, QT prolongation or arrhythmia
Replace magnesium before expecting potassium or calcium to correct
Review diuretics, proton pump inhibitors, cisplatin, aminoglycosides and calcineurin inhibitors as reversible causes
In severe deficiency or arrhythmia, give IV magnesium and monitor reflexes and blood pressure

differential.name: Hypokalemia
differential.why_considered: Weakness, cramps, palpitations and arrhythmia are shared, and low potassium and low magnesium very often occur together.
differential.trigger: Unexplained weakness or arrhythmia with a low potassium that will not correct despite replacement

history: Muscle weakness that is worse in the legs
labs: Low serum potassium with normal magnesium
Low urine potassium in poor intake
ecg: Flattened T waves with prominent U waves

differential.name: Hypocalcemia
differential.why_considered: Perioral and acral paresthesia, cramps, carpopedal spasm and seizures are classic for both, and hypocalcemia often accompanies hypomagnesemia.
differential.trigger: Positive Trousseau or Chvostek sign with paresthesia or tetany

history: Chronic kidney disease or vitamin D deficiency
labs: Low total or ionized calcium with normal magnesium

differential.name: Hypothyroidism
differential.why_considered: Fatigue, muscle cramps, weakness and cognitive slowing overlap with hypomagnesemia.

exam: Delayed relaxation of deep tendon reflexes
labs: Elevated TSH with low free T4

differential.name: Hypoparathyroidism
differential.why_considered: Causes hypocalcemia with paresthesia, cramps, tetany and seizures that mimic severe hypomagnesemia.

labs: Low calcium with low or inappropriately normal PTH
Low magnesium may cause functional hypoparathyroidism and should be corrected first

differential.name: Periodic paralysis
differential.why_considered: Episodic generalized weakness and cramps can resemble hypomagnesemia, especially with coexisting electrolyte shifts.

history: Episodes after carbohydrate-rich meals, rest or exercise
Attacks are episodic rather than continuous
labs: Low potassium during attacks in hypokalemic periodic paralysis

differential.name: Alcohol withdrawal
differential.why_considered: Tremor, agitation, confusion, seizures and autonomic hyperactivity overlap with severe hypomagnesemia, and both are common in alcohol use disorder.

history: Recent cessation or reduction of heavy drinking
Autonomic symptoms beginning hours after last drink
labs: Low magnesium is common but not the primary cause

differential.name: Medication-induced tremor or myoclonus
differential.why_considered: Tremor, twitching and agitation from stimulants, beta-agonists, theophylline or lithium can be mistaken for hypomagnesemia.

history: Temporal relationship to a new medication or dose increase
Use of albuterol, theophylline, lithium or stimulants

severity.mild: Serum magnesium 1.3–1.7 mg/dL; vague fatigue, mild cramps or no symptoms; no ECG changes.
severity.moderate: Serum magnesium 1.0–1.3 mg/dL; prominent cramps, twitching, paresthesia, hyperreflexia, QT prolongation or atrial arrhythmia.
severity.severe: Serum magnesium 0.7–1.0 mg/dL; carpopedal spasm, tetany, seizures, ventricular arrhythmia or hypotension.
severity.critical: Serum magnesium below 0.7 mg/dL with torsades de pointes, ventricular fibrillation, refractory seizures or shock.

red_flags.finding: Torsades de pointes or sustained ventricular arrhythmia
red_flags.meaning: Life-threatening; give IV magnesium immediately and stabilize.
Severe deficiency with neuromuscular irritability; urgent IV replacement.
Risk of torsades; correct magnesium and potassium before other measures.
May reflect arrhythmia or coexisting volume and electrolyte disturbance.

red_flags.finding: Hypokalemia or hypocalcemia that does not correct with replacement
red_flags.meaning: Suggests underlying hypomagnesemia that must be treated first.

complications.name: Cardiac arrhythmia including atrial fibrillation and torsades de pointes
Refractory hypokalemia and hypocalcemia
clues: Potassium or calcium remains low despite replacement

special_populations.differences: Symptoms are often attributed to aging or other chronic illness; weakness, confusion and falls may be the only clues, and arrhythmia risk is higher.
May present with irritability, poor feeding, vomiting, muscle twitching or seizures rather than clear cramps.
Leg cramps and nausea are common in pregnancy, so hypomagnesemia may be missed; severe deficiency can cause tetany or preterm contractions.
Magnesium wasting from tubular injury or diuretics can coexist with kidney disease; symptoms may be masked by uremia and magnesium replacement must be monitored closely.
Osmotic diuresis from hyperglycemia causes renal magnesium loss; symptoms overlap with hypoglycemia and neuropathy.

key_questions.question: What medications are you taking, including any water pills, stomach acid medicines, or chemotherapy?
key_questions.looking_for: Loop or thiazide diuretics, proton pump inhibitors, cisplatin, aminoglycosides, amphotericin B, calcineurin inhibitors, or insulin — all cause renal magnesium loss

key_questions.question: How much alcohol do you drink, and have you recently cut down or stopped?
key_questions.looking_for: Heavy use or recent withdrawal; alcohol use disorder is a strong risk factor and withdrawal can mimic the neuromuscular findings

key_questions.question: Have you had diarrhea, vomiting, or trouble keeping food down?
key_questions.looking_for: Chronic diarrhea or malabsorption causing gastrointestinal magnesium loss; vomiting also causes renal wasting

key_questions.question: How has your appetite and diet been?
key_questions.looking_for: Poor oral intake, malnutrition or food insecurity as a cause of low magnesium

key_questions.question: Have you noticed muscle cramps, twitching, or tingling around your mouth or in your hands and feet?
key_questions.looking_for: Neuromuscular irritability — cramps, fasciculations, perioral or acral paresthesia — suggesting moderate to severe deficiency

key_questions.question: Have you had palpitations, a fluttering feeling, or fainting?
key_questions.looking_for: Arrhythmia such as atrial fibrillation or torsades; changes urgency of treatment

key_questions.question: Have you had any seizures or episodes of confusion?
key_questions.looking_for: Seizure or altered mental status indicating severe deficiency requiring urgent IV replacement

key_questions.question: Do you have diabetes, and how well controlled is your blood sugar?
key_questions.looking_for: Poorly controlled diabetes with glycosuria causing osmotic renal magnesium loss

key_questions.question: Do you have kidney disease or heart failure?
key_questions.looking_for: Chronic kidney disease or heart failure — affects magnesium handling, diuretic use, and replacement dosing

key_questions.question: Has anyone in your family had similar problems with low magnesium or electrolyte imbalances?
key_questions.looking_for: Inherited tubulopathies such as Gitelman syndrome causing renal magnesium wasting

key_questions.question: Have you had any recent chemotherapy or IV antibiotics?
key_questions.looking_for: Cisplatin, aminoglycosides, or amphotericin B — all cause renal magnesium wasting

key_questions.question: Have you had any recent surgery, especially on your thyroid or parathyroid?
key_questions.looking_for: Post-surgical hypoparathyroidism causing hypocalcemia that mimics hypomagnesemia

reasoning_points: Serum magnesium below the normal range confirms the diagnosis and grades severity
Review of medications identifies reversible causes: diuretics, proton pump inhibitors, cisplatin, aminoglycosides, amphotericin B, calcineurin inhibitors
History of alcohol use disorder, chronic diarrhea, or poor oral intake points to the cause
Neuromuscular irritability (cramps, twitching, paresthesia, Trousseau or Chvostek sign) supports moderate to severe deficiency
ECG findings of QT prolongation, flattened T waves, or atrial arrhythmia raise concern for cardiac complications
Coexisting hypokalemia or hypocalcemia that is refractory to replacement suggests underlying hypomagnesemia
Urine magnesium and specific gravity help distinguish renal wasting from poor intake when the cause is unclear
Severe deficiency with tetany, seizures, or arrhythmia requires urgent IV magnesium replacement

easy: Patient on a loop diuretic with classic muscle cramps and twitching
Serum magnesium clearly below normal range
Coexisting hypokalemia that will not correct
medium: Older adult on long-term proton pump inhibitor with vague weakness and fatigue
Patient with alcohol use disorder presenting with tremor and confusion
Coexisting hypocalcemia with paresthesia and positive Trousseau sign
Atrial fibrillation with no other obvious cause
hard: Normal serum magnesium but clinical suspicion of deficiency (intracellular depletion)
Patient with chronic diarrhea and multiple electrolyte abnormalities
Renal impairment masking symptoms and complicating replacement
Pregnancy with leg cramps attributed to normal pregnancy
Child with irritability, poor feeding, and seizures
